<reason>High-quality, format-compliant debate on both sides. A built the stronger new-build attack (Vogtle/Hinkley/Flamanville never substantively disputed; UAE/Korea comparability critique landed; modularity-vs-cascade was a fresh systems frame) and asked the sharpest single question (Q2), which B could only answer by pivoting to Darlington refurbishment. But B held the motion as written: it weaponized A's opening concession that life extension is "genuinely cheap," neutralized the "preservation isn't abatement" move ("bookkeeping, not physics; avoided is avoided"), and — decisively — answered A's "capped" attack with a magnitude claim (US fleet, France, Japan restarts, Ontario = tens of GW rivaling a decade of wind, delivered immediately) that A never engaged, only re-labeled. B's timing ledger (extension abates in year one; solar's first ton arrives after queues) was the cleanest weighing device in the debate and survived unneutralized; A's "scale-up" requirement was a partial reframe that B textually checked ("the motion joins them with and"). Germany's counterfactual also went wholly unanswered by A. A's closing "averaging" argument was its best counterweight but came after B's frame had hardened. B's path to victory remained live; A's required accepting its reframe over the motion text.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1: converting A's "genuinely cheap" concession into the core of the motion, dismantling the "not new abatement" distinction with the Germany counterfactual, and exposing A's nameplate-per-MW pricing versus delivered, firmed megawatt-hours — a frame A never priced its way out of across the remaining speeches.</best_rebuttal>
